literalGroups.primaryGround: All four labels name Russian rulers. The source frames the Kremlin fortress/wall and tower rebuilding in Ivan III's reign and around the turn of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries; retained primary pages date Ivan IV's Kazan campaign to 1552, Peter I's Senate to 1711, and Alexander I's ministries to 1802. Ivan III is the unique ruler matching the Kremlin construction fact.

literalGroups.primaryGround: The official Kremlin teaching material places the fortress at the turn of the fifteenth/sixteenth centuries, names Italian architects, and describes brick walls/towers. In its Ivan III section it dates his rule and the Kremlin rebuilding; the Museum page identifies him as builder of the brick Kremlin and distinguishes later completion work.

literalGroups.primaryGround: The retained Presidential Library page describes Ivan IV's 1552 campaign and capture of Kazan on 2 (12) October; this is a concrete fact about Ivan IV and distinguishes his sixteenth-century reign from Kremlin construction under Ivan III.

literalGroups.primaryGround: The retained Presidential Library page states that Peter I established the Governing Senate in 1711; this is a concrete fact about Peter I and distinguishes the eighteenth-century ruler from Ivan III.

literalGroups.literal: При Иване III в конце XV века возвели нынешние кирпичные стены Московского Кремля.

literalGroups.literal: Александр I учредил министерства в России в 1802 году.
literalGroups.primaryGround: The retained Presidential Library page states that Alexander I's 8 (20) September 1802 manifesto created eight ministries; this is a concrete fact about Alexander I and distinguishes his nineteenth-century reign from Ivan III.

absoluteDifficulty.audienceGround: A Russian-history enthusiast or adult regularly familiar with national history is likely to recognize Ivan III as the ruler associated with the late-fifteenth-century brick Kremlin. An adult outside that topic can narrow four plausible Russian rulers by period but cannot identify the answer from absurd distractors alone.
absoluteDifficulty.judgment: This tests thematic familiarity, not a widely shared adult fact (easy) or a specialist detail/multistep inference (hard). All three distractors are real Russian rulers and their notes teach independently grounded historical facts.

limitations: The official teaching page expresses the fortress date as the turn of the fifteenth/sixteenth centuries; the current note says late fifteenth century. The official Museum page identifies Ivan III as builder of the brick Kremlin and clarifies that associated work continued after his death. No claim is made that every related Kremlin project was complete before Ivan III died.
